Yet, among plausible explanations for this specific constellation — chronic osmotic diuresis + hypokalemic hypochloremic electrolyte pattern + absence of red flags for alternatives (e.g., no hypertension or hypokalemic alkalosis to suggest mineralocorticoid excess; no confusion or seizures to suggest severe hyponatremia or SIADH; no fatigue/melanosis/hypotension for adrenal insufficiency) — undiagnosed T2DM is the single most likely underlying diagnosis.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Chronic (months) polyuria and polydipsia — hallmark symptoms of persistent hyperglycemia  
- Generalized weakness — common nonspecific symptom of chronic hyperglycemia and electrolyte depletion  
- Hyponatremia (Na⁺ = 135 mEq/L) — consistent with pseudohyponatremia from hyperglycemia and/or concomitant urinary sodium loss  
- Hypokalemia (K⁺ = 3.2 mEq/L) — reflects true renal potassium wasting due to osmotic diuresis and intracellular shift during eventual insulin correction  
- Hypochloremia (Cl⁻ = 95 mEq/L) — aligns with urinary chloride loss in chronic glucosuric diuresis  
- Absence of weight loss, visual changes, or recurrent infections — favors indolent, uncomplicated T2DM over acute T1DM or advanced disease  

[GAPS]  
- Serum or capillary glucose level (fasting/random) — required to confirm hyperglycemia  
- HbA1c — needed to establish chronicity of hyperglycemia  
- Urine or blood ketones — essential to rule out ketosis-prone diabetes (e.g., T1DM or ketosis-prone T2DM)  
- Serum bicarbonate or venous blood gas — necessary to assess for metabolic acidosis (e.g., DKA)  
- Urinalysis for glucose and ketones — rapid, accessible confirmation of glucosuria  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
